summary: A local news piece assessing how well the city's public transit systems comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) as of late 2023. It describes gaps in maintenance, staff training, rural service and feedback channels, uneven FTA enforcement, and limited funding. It also notes technology improvements and ongoing efforts, concluding that compliance is a continuing commitment rather than a finish line.
one_line: A late-2023 local report finds ADA compliance in city transit uneven, citing maintenance, training, funding and enforcement gaps, while technology and community engagement offer progress.
key_facts: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was introduced in 1990 and mandates that transit agencies make their services accessible to all.
On September 15th, 2023, visually-impaired commuter Emily Johnston found an out-of-service elevator at her regular subway station and had to rely on strangers to reach an unfamiliar bus route.
Michael Anderson, a wheelchair user and frequent bus rider, said that when drivers don't know how to secure his chair, it delays everyone and is unsafe.
From September 1st to October 10th, 2023, Transportation Access for All (TAA), led by Maria Sanchez, carried out surveys and inspections of transit accessibility.

TAA identified recurring issues: broken lifts or escalators, inoperative real-time information services, service gaps in less-populated areas, and a lack of systematic feedback mechanisms for reporting problems.
The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) is tasked with ADA enforcement, but some argue it favors compliance assistance over strict enforcement.
Sarah Gibson of Disabled Rights Action Committee argues that "without real consequences, ADA compliance will always take a backseat to other priorities."
On September 21st, 2023, Sister Margaret Ryan, chair of the local transit board's accessibility subcommittee, acknowledged that coverage and response times for reported issues could be more robust.
On September 25th, 2023, the city council approved a modest increase in funding specifically earmarked for ADA improvements.
Economist Lawrence Fisher said the cost of not investing in accessibility can be far higher long term due to lost productivity and potential legal liabilities.
On October 1st, 2023, city transportation head Daniel Rosen announced a roll-out of new GPS systems on buses to give riders with disabilities real-time data on outages and delays.
Some city council members have floated public-private partnerships or dedicated local taxes as ways to close the financing gap.
Mike Roberts, director of the Center for Accessible Living, said every broken elevator or missed staff training session is a barrier to independence.
